title: Currency transaction reporting threshold
text: Financial institutions in the United States must file a Currency Transaction Report for any cash transaction, or series of related cash transactions by the same customer on the same business day, exceeding USD 10,000. The obligation is mechanical: it applies regardless of whether the institution regards the activity as suspicious. Deliberately splitting funds to remain below this figure is a separate criminal offence and does not remove the reporting duty.

title: Suspicious activity reporting obligation
text: Where an institution suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, that funds are proceeds of crime or relate to terrorist financing, it must promptly file a report with the national Financial Intelligence Unit. The standard is suspicion, not proof, and no monetary threshold applies. An institution must not disclose to the customer that a report has been filed, as this constitutes unlawful tipping-off.

title: Wire transfer originator information requirement
text: Cross-border wire transfers must carry accurate originator and beneficiary information, including name, account number and address or national identity number. Institutions must monitor for transfers lacking required fields and should treat missing or manifestly false originator data as a risk indicator warranting further review before execution.

title: Threshold avoidance as an independent offence
text: Structuring transactions for the purpose of evading a reporting requirement is itself unlawful, independent of whether the underlying funds are criminal in origin. Detection typically rests on clustering of amounts immediately beneath the reporting threshold, particularly where the pattern recurs across days, branches or related accounts.

title: Structuring typology definition
text: Structuring is the deliberate division of a large sum into multiple smaller transactions, each individually below a regulatory reporting threshold, in order to avoid triggering a report. The defining signature is not the size of any single transaction but the arithmetic relationship between the transactions: several deposits that individually appear unremarkable but which aggregate to a substantial total over a short window.

title: Structuring red flags
text: Indicators include repeated cash amounts falling just under the reporting threshold, deposits made across several branches on the same day, transactions timed to fall on consecutive business days, amounts that are conspicuously round, and a customer who asks staff what the reporting threshold is or who reduces a transaction when informed a report will be filed.

title: Distinguishing structuring from legitimate patterns
text: Some businesses legitimately deposit frequent moderate cash sums, notably retail, hospitality and cash-intensive services. The distinguishing feature of structuring is that amounts cluster immediately beneath the threshold rather than distributing naturally around the business's normal takings. A genuine retail depositor's amounts vary with trade; a structurer's amounts vary only enough to avoid appearing identical.

title: Smurfing typology definition
text: Smurfing distributes a criminal sum across multiple individuals, each of whom conducts transactions on behalf of the principal. Where structuring divides the amount, smurfing divides the people. The funds are later consolidated into a single account or beneficiary. Detection requires a network view, since each individual participant's activity may appear entirely ordinary in isolation.

title: Smurfing red flags
text: Warning signs include multiple unrelated individuals depositing similar amounts into a single beneficiary account, participants sharing an address, telephone number or employer, deposits made in rapid succession at the same branch by different people, and depositors whose stated income or occupation is inconsistent with the sums handled.

title: Layering stage of money laundering
text: Layering is the second stage of laundering, following placement and preceding integration. Its purpose is to sever the audit trail between funds and their criminal source by moving them through successive transfers, accounts, instruments or jurisdictions. Each individual transfer may be lawful on its face; the illicit character emerges only from the sequence and its lack of economic purpose.

title: Layered fan-out pattern
text: In a layered fan-out, funds move from one origin account to several intermediate accounts, and from each of those to further accounts, forming successive tiers. Transaction values commonly decrease by a margin of roughly ten to twenty percent at each layer as intermediaries retain a fee. The multi-tier depth distinguishes it from a simple fan-out.

title: Layered fan-in pattern
text: A layered fan-in reverses the fan-out direction: many source accounts transmit to a smaller set of intermediaries, which in turn consolidate into a single destination account. It is characteristic of the consolidation phase, where dispersed funds are reassembled before integration into the legitimate economy.

title: Cycle and round-trip transfers
text: A cycle occurs when funds depart an account and return to it through a chain of intermediaries, producing a closed loop. The absence of any net economic change combined with transaction costs incurred along the path indicates the movement served an obfuscation purpose rather than a commercial one.

title: Scatter-gather and gather-scatter patterns
text: Scatter-gather disperses funds from a single account to many recipients, then reassembles them at a different single account. Gather-scatter reverses the order, first pooling from many sources and then redistributing. Both create a deliberate many-to-many segment that frustrates simple linear trace analysis.

title: Bipartite and stacked bipartite structures
text: Bipartite structures route funds between two distinct groups of accounts with no transfers within either group. Stacking repeats this arrangement across several successive stages. The rigid group separation is itself anomalous, since organic transaction networks normally show some intra-group activity.

title: Money mule account characteristics
text: A money mule receives funds into a personal account and forwards them onward, usually retaining a small commission. Mule accounts are commonly newly opened, held by younger or financially inexperienced individuals, and show near-zero balance retention as incoming credits are withdrawn or transferred within hours. Recruitment frequently occurs through fraudulent job advertisements.

title: Pass-through and rapid movement indicators
text: Pass-through behaviour is indicated where the interval between credit and onward debit is very short, where outgoing amounts closely mirror incoming ones, and where the account maintains no meaningful balance between events. Absence of ordinary personal spending on an account that nonetheless handles substantial throughput is a strong indicator.

title: Deposit-send typology
text: In the deposit-send typology an account receives a cash deposit and transmits the funds onward within a short period, frequently to a higher-risk jurisdiction. Deposit amounts commonly sit below the reporting threshold. The rapid conversion of cash into an outbound transfer is the operative risk signal, as it compresses the placement and layering stages.

title: Cash intensity risk
text: Cash is the highest-risk medium in laundering because it carries no inherent transaction record. Elevated risk arises where cash activity is inconsistent with the customer's declared business, where a customer with no cash-generating occupation makes regular cash deposits, or where deposits substantially exceed the volumes typical for the stated sector.

title: Unusual cash deposit red flags
text: Indicators include deposits in unusually worn or uniformly sequenced notes, deposits made by third parties into an account they do not control, deposits at branches remote from the customer's residence or place of business, and sudden commencement of cash activity on an account with a prior history of electronic transactions only.

title: Suspicious cash withdrawal patterns
text: Repeated low-value cash withdrawals can indicate distribution of criminal proceeds where individual amounts fall beneath monitoring thresholds. Such patterns are associated with exploitation offences and informal payment networks. The aggregate withdrawn over a period, rather than any single withdrawal, carries the signal.

title: High-risk jurisdiction exposure
source: FATF high-risk and monitored jurisdictions lists
text: FATF maintains public lists of jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies in their anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing regimes. Transactions involving listed jurisdictions require enhanced scrutiny. Exposure alone does not establish suspicion, but it raises the applicable due diligence standard and must be documented in the risk assessment.

title: Currency mismatch and corridor anomalies
text: A mismatch between payment currency and receiving currency, or a transfer corridor unrelated to the customer's known commercial footprint, warrants examination. Legitimate cross-border trade generally follows stable corridors tied to identifiable counterparties; sudden appearance of an unrelated corridor is anomalous.

title: Over-invoicing and trade-based laundering
text: Trade-based laundering transfers value by misstating the price, quantity or quality of goods on invoices. Over-invoicing moves value to the exporter by overstating worth; under-invoicing moves it to the importer. Indicators include prices materially divergent from market rates, goods inconsistent with the parties' stated business, and payment routed through a jurisdiction unconnected to either party.

title: Correspondent banking and nested relationships
text: Correspondent relationships carry elevated risk because the correspondent institution does not maintain a direct relationship with the respondent's underlying customers. Institutions must gather sufficient information about a respondent to understand its business and reputation, and must refuse relationships with shell banks or where nested access is provided without disclosure.

title: Customer due diligence requirements
text: Institutions must identify the customer and verify identity using reliable independent source documents, identify any beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify that identity, understand the purpose and intended nature of the relationship, and conduct ongoing due diligence to ensure transactions remain consistent with the institution's knowledge of the customer and their risk profile.

title: Enhanced due diligence triggers
text: Enhanced due diligence is required for politically exposed persons, customers established in higher-risk jurisdictions, complex or unusually large transactions lacking apparent economic purpose, and non-face-to-face relationships. Enhanced measures include obtaining senior management approval, establishing source of funds and source of wealth, and applying increased ongoing monitoring.

title: Risk rating and transaction consistency
text: Customers should carry a documented risk rating derived from occupation, geography, product usage and expected activity. A transaction is anomalous when it is inconsistent with that expected profile. A high-risk rating does not by itself make any individual transaction suspicious; it lowers the threshold at which deviation warrants investigation.

title: Beneficial ownership opacity
text: Legal persons and arrangements can be used to obscure the identity of the natural person who ultimately owns or controls funds. Risk indicators include ownership chains spanning multiple jurisdictions without commercial rationale, nominee arrangements, bearer instruments, and reluctance or inability to provide ownership information on request.

title: Source of funds and source of wealth
text: Source of funds refers to the origin of the specific money used in a transaction; source of wealth refers to the origin of the customer's total accumulated assets. The two are distinct and both may be required for higher-risk customers. An explanation that cannot be evidenced, or that is inconsistent with the customer's known occupation and history, is an adverse indicator.

title: New account risk
text: Recently opened accounts carry elevated risk because the institution has not yet observed a baseline of normal behaviour. Substantial activity commencing shortly after opening, particularly where it exceeds the volumes anticipated at onboarding, should be reviewed against the customer's stated purpose for the account.

title: Behavioural change indicators
text: A material departure from an account's established pattern is a primary monitoring signal. Relevant changes include a sharp rise in transaction frequency or value, the appearance of counterparties with no prior relationship, a shift into new payment channels, and movement into geographies the customer has not previously transacted with.

title: Behavioural change into high-risk geography
text: Where an established account begins transacting with new counterparties located in higher-risk jurisdictions, the combination of counterparty novelty and geographic risk is more significant than either factor alone. This composite pattern is treated as a distinct typology in transaction-monitoring practice.

title: Single large transaction anomaly
text: An isolated transaction of a magnitude far exceeding an account's historical range warrants review even where no other indicator is present. The assessment turns on whether a documented economic rationale exists, such as a property sale or inheritance, and whether that rationale can be evidenced.

title: Round-amount transactions
text: Genuine commercial payments usually carry irregular values reflecting prices, taxes and fees. A persistent pattern of round figures suggests amounts determined by an internal allocation rather than by trade. Round amounts are weak evidence alone but gain weight in combination with threshold proximity or rapid onward movement.

title: Velocity and frequency anomalies
text: Transaction velocity measures how many transactions an account conducts within a defined window. A sudden increase relative to the account's own history, or relative to peers in the same segment, is a recognised alert trigger. Velocity is evaluated together with value, since many small rapid transfers and few large ones carry different typology implications.

title: Prior alert history as a risk factor
text: Accounts with previously raised alerts, including alerts closed without a report, warrant a lower threshold for subsequent review. Repeated alerting across time is itself a pattern. Prior alerts do not establish that current activity is suspicious and must not be treated as substituting for analysis of the present transaction.

title: Dormant account reactivation
text: Reactivation of a long-dormant account followed by significant transaction volume is a recognised indicator, as dormant accounts are attractive to third parties seeking an established banking history without an active owner monitoring the account. Verification of continued genuine customer control is warranted.

title: Linked account clustering
text: Accounts sharing identifying attributes such as address, device, telephone number or common counterparties may form a controlled cluster. Analysis at cluster level can reveal aggregate patterns invisible at the level of any individual account, including structuring distributed across nominally unrelated holders.

title: Periodic and salary transaction baselines
text: Regular transfers of stable value at consistent intervals, such as salary credits, rent debits and utility payments, form the normal baseline of retail accounts. Their regularity is exculpatory rather than suspicious. Monitoring systems should model these patterns explicitly to reduce false positives.

title: Legitimate mutual and reciprocal activity
text: Recurring two-way transfers between the same pair of accounts commonly reflect shared household expenses, informal lending between acquaintances or ordinary commercial settlement. This pattern is distinguishable from cycling because it does not traverse a chain of intermediaries and does not return to origin through third parties.

title: False positive burden in rules-based monitoring
text: Conventional rules-based transaction monitoring generates very high false positive rates, frequently cited at around ninety-five percent of alerts. This imposes substantial investigative cost and creates a risk that genuine cases are lost among unproductive alerts. Reducing false positives without reducing detection is a central objective of automated approaches.
